::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
You will measure forest damage from Tropical Cyclone Seroja in Nusa Tenggara Timur by comparing canopy moisture before and after the storm, and you will learn why a before/after comparison is not enough unless the same weeks of a normal year are subtracted. You will also see a second sensor fail to confirm the result, and what to make of that.
:::

## The storm

Seroja formed over the Savu Sea and struck Nusa Tenggara Timur on 4–5 April 2021, with extreme rain, floods and landslides as well as wind. Rote, Sumba and Timor were all hit, Rote among the hardest. Wind damage to forest takes several forms: leaves stripped, branches and crowns broken, trees snapped or uprooted. Each lowers the amount of green, water-filled leaf the canopy holds.

## Separating the wind from the season

The **NDMI** (normalised difference moisture index, from near infrared and shortwave infrared) tracks canopy water. A storm that strips and breaks the canopy lowers it. But Seroja came at the turn from the wet to the dry season, when canopies in Nusa Tenggara dry anyway. A simple before/after drop would blame the wind for the season.

The fix is a **baseline year**. Measure the change across the same weeks in a year without a cyclone (2020) and subtract it:

$$\text{anomaly} = (\text{after} - \text{before})_{2021} - (\text{after} - \text{before})_{2020}$$

This follows the author's wind-damage analysis (indices before and after, summarised per stand), with the baseline added. "Before" is February to March, "after" mid-April to May, from cloud-masked Sentinel-2 surface reflectance, on ESA WorldCover tree cover.

{{< include _snippets/ch46_windstorm.qmd >}}

## Reading the results

**Rote.** The forest's NDMI fell across April 2021 far more than across the same weeks of 2020: the median anomaly is −0.066, and about a third of the forest (32 %, about 15,800 ha) has an anomaly below −0.1. The histogram shows it is not a few damaged patches: the whole distribution shifts.

**The gradient.** On east Sumba the median anomaly is −0.012, in West Timor around Kupang −0.004. In both, about one forest pixel in six falls below −0.1, roughly what noise and patchy cloud masking produce on their own. The damage signal is strongest where the cyclone passed closest.

**Per block.** The 1 km block map is the form a forest agency would use: where to inspect, where salvage or replanting may be needed.

**Radar did not confirm it.** Sentinel-1 VH backscatter changed by almost nothing on any of the three islands. One likely reason is that C-band radar responds to the volume and structure of branches and stems more than to leaf moisture, so stripped leaves alone barely move it. Whatever the reason, the honest report says: one sensor shows clear damage on Rote, a second sensor does not. Field photographs or very-high-resolution images of a sample of blocks would settle it.

## How much does the answer depend on my choices?

Three choices shaped the result: the baseline year, the index and the −0.1 threshold. A careful analyst changes each one and watches what moves.

**The baseline year.** Without a baseline, 46 % of Rote's forest looks damaged. With 2020 as the baseline it is 32 %, with 2019 42 %, with 2023 37 % and with 2022 only 24 %. Every baseline still gives a negative median anomaly (−0.04 to −0.08), so the existence of damage is robust. Its size is not: it changes by a factor of almost two depending on which "normal" year you pick. No single year is normal. The honest fix is to use the average of several baseline years and report the spread.

**The index.** With NDVI, the signal almost disappears. The median anomaly sits near zero for most baselines, and the share below −0.1 is between 7 % and 24 %. That fits the physics: a stripped and broken canopy loses water before it loses greenness, and the undergrowth and grass greening beneath it can mask the loss. NDMI sees canopy water through the shortwave infrared, and here that is the better witness. As in @sec-oil-palm-age, the index is a choice you test, not a habit.

**The threshold.** What counts as "damaged"? Lower the bar to −0.03 and 68 % of Rote's forest is flagged, but so is 39 % of West Timor's. Raise it to −0.2 and only 7 % of Rote is flagged. The useful threshold is not the one that gives the biggest number. It is the one that best separates the cyclone track from a comparison area.

The table and chart show two ways to read that separation:

- **The difference** (Rote minus West Timor) estimates *how much* excess damage there is. It is largest at loose thresholds: 29 percentage points at −0.03, falling to 4 at −0.2.
- **The ratio** (Rote divided by West Timor) estimates *how clean* the flag is. It rises from 1.7 at −0.03 to 2.1 at −0.2.

There is no single optimum; it is a trade-off:

- **To estimate total damaged area,** use a loose threshold (−0.05) and subtract the comparison rate.
- **To send field teams to blocks that are almost certainly damaged,** use a strict one (−0.15 or −0.2).

With −0.05, the excess over West Timor is about 26 % of Rote's roughly 50,000 ha of forest, or 13,000 ha.

One more caution. West Timor is not undamaged: Kupang itself was hit hard by Seroja. A comparison area that also suffered makes the excess an underestimate. A cleaner design would take a comparison area of similar forest well outside the storm's path.

## Verdict: how far to trust this, and how to make it accurate

**Verdict.** The method is fast: two seasonal composites, one subtraction, minutes in Earth Engine. It is excellent for learning, because it teaches the single most important idea in change detection: separate the event from the season. As a damage assessment it is **indicative, not accurate**:

- Damage is clearly present on Rote under every baseline and threshold.
- Its extent ranges from about 24 % to 46 % of the forest depending on defensible choices.
- Radar did not confirm it.
- No field data was used.

Use it to decide where to look, not to state hectares in a report to an insurer or a ministry.

**What a funded assessment would do to make it accurate:**

1. **Field plots and damage classes.** Visit a stratified sample of blocks (strong, moderate and no anomaly) and record the share of trees defoliated, broken or uprooted. This turns the anomaly into a calibrated damage class and gives a real accuracy figure.
2. **Very-high-resolution imagery or drone surveys.** Look before and after, at sub-metre resolution, on the same sample. Snapped and uprooted crowns are visible directly. This is the fastest substitute for field plots.
3. **LiDAR or stereo canopy height before and after.** Height loss measures structural damage that moisture indices miss once leaves regrow. Where pre-storm LiDAR exists, a repeat flight is the gold standard.
4. **A multi-year baseline.** Average 2018–2020 (and 2022–2023 if the forest recovered) and report the spread, instead of trusting one year.
5. **A proper control.** Choose comparison forest of the same type outside the storm track, or model the expected change from rainfall and phenology.
6. **L-band radar.** ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 penetrates deeper into the canopy than C-band. It responds to broken stems and branches, the damage Sentinel-1 could not see here.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Replace the single baseline year with the mean change of 2018–2020. Report the Rote damage share with the minimum and maximum across those years.
2. Pick a comparison forest well outside the storm's path, for example in Flores or central Sumba. Does the excess damage on Rote grow once the comparison area is truly undamaged?
3. Sample 50 blocks with the strongest anomaly and look at them in high-resolution basemaps from before and after. How many show visible damage?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

**1.** The chapter already gives the pieces: the Rote damage share is 42 % with 2019 as the baseline and 32 % with 2020. Add 2018, average the three baseline changes, and subtract the mean. The single-year results span the minimum and maximum. Expect the mean-baseline share to sit in the middle (roughly a third of the forest). Report that spread with it; a reader can then see how much of the number is the choice of year.

**2.** Not computed in the chapter. Choose forest of a similar type far from the track, for example on Flores, and compute its share below each threshold. If the comparison rate drops below West Timor's (17 % at −0.1), the excess on Rote grows. That would confirm that West Timor was itself damaged and that the chapter's 13,000 ha is an underestimate.

**3.** This one has no computed answer: it is a visual check you must do. Use a before/after pair at sub-metre resolution, and score each block blind (without looking at its anomaly first) as visibly damaged, unclear or undamaged. The share of "visibly damaged" in the strongest-anomaly blocks is a first precision estimate. Do the same for 50 random forest blocks as the comparison.
:::
